clue.text: Slayer of Titus is Cronos in America

parts.note: Cronos, the Greek Titan, is identified with the Roman god Saturn
taken as written

explanation.surface: A note on who killed Titus, with a Greek god somehow transplanted to America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is only a link. Saturninus, Roman emperor in Titus Andronicus, stabs Titus in the final scene.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's tragedy the emperor Saturninus kills Titus Andronicus at the banquet.

clue.text: Where Othello stabbed a malignant Turk

definitions.text: Where Othello stabbed a malignant Turk

parts.words: Where Othello stabbed a malignant Turk
parts.note: Othello's last speech recalls that in this Syrian city a malignant and turbaned Turk beat a Venetian, and he smote him

explanation.surface: A question about the place of one of Othello's remembered killings.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue simply recalls Othello's dying speech, where he names the city in which he struck down the Turk.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello's final speech sets the incident 'in Aleppo once', naming the Syrian city directly.

clue.text: Illegal, like Enright's collection

definitions.meaning: D. J. Enright's poetry collection was titled ... Assembly

explanation.surface: A remark that a poet's book is somehow against the law.
explanation.definitionFit: Something illegal is against the law, and Enright's book title begins with that same adjective.

clue.text: Nothing novel in this category

parts.note: read literally, a category with no novel in it: the bookshop section for factual prose rather than invented stories

explanation.surface: A complaint that a category offers nothing new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like 'new', but it means a work of invented fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: The bookshop category of factual writing contains no novels by definition.

clue.text: Satrap of Alexander put some foes in panic — a normal reaction

indicators.note: some means only a portion of the following words is used, the letters running across them

explanation.surface: An ancient governor sends enemies into a panic, and that is the expected response.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'paNIC A NORmal'. Nicanor was one of Alexander the Great's officers given a satrapy, a provincial governorship.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicanor was a Macedonian officer appointed provincial governor (satrap) under Alexander the Great.

clue.text: French confirmation party for Colette's mother

parts.note: si is French for 'yes', used to affirm against a negative
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A French church confirmation celebration held for the novelist's mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confirmation' suggests the church rite but means saying yes. Colette wrote a memoir of her mother, Sidonie, titled Sido.
explanation.definitionFit: Colette's mother Sidonie was known as Sido, the title of Colette's memoir of her.

clue.text: Desdemona's uncle from The Merchant of Venice

definitions.meaning: in Othello, Brabantio's brother, who appears in the final act
a talkative friend of Bassanio in that play, who marries Nerissa

explanation.surface: Shakespeare characters confused: Desdemona's uncle apparently borrowed from another Venetian play.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare used the same name for two characters in his two Venetian plays.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare gave one name to Brabantio's brother in Othello and to Bassanio's companion in the Venice comedy.

clue.text: Maugham artist suggests illusion in southern country

indicators.note: in means the word for illusion is placed inside the other pieces

parts.note: a land is a country
a trick is an illusion

explanation.surface: A Maugham painter hints at some deception in a land in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suggests' is only a link. The painter is the hero of Maugham's The Moon and Sixpence, modelled on Gauguin.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Strickland is the painter at the centre of Maugham's novel The Moon and Sixpence.

clue.text: Many a dome and fair-roofed — (Thomas Moore, Lalla Rookh)

definitions.text: Many a dome and fair-roofed — (Thomas Moore, Lalla Rookh)

parts.words: Many a dome and fair-roofed — (Thomas Moore, Lalla Rookh)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation: Moore's line ends with a Turkish word for a hospice or almshouse

explanation.surface: A gap-filling line from Thomas Moore's oriental poem Lalla Rookh.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is a Turkish term for a charitable hospice, which Moore uses in an Eastern scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Moore's line completes as 'many a dome and fair-roofed imaret', a Turkish hospice for travellers.

clue.text: Greek Hades not quite nice

parts.note: Hades, the underworld, is hell

indicators.note: not quite suggests the word nice is altered, its letters shuffled out of their order

explanation.surface: A remark that the Greek underworld is less than pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' turns NICE into ENIC.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things of Greece or the ancient Greeks.

clue.text: Accord new merit to a collection of Spenser's love sonnets

indicators.note: new signals the letters are made into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Give fresh credit to a book of Spenser's love poems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accord' is only a link; 'new' rearranges MERIT, TO and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser's sonnet sequence courting Elizabeth Boyle is titled with the Italian word for little loves.

clue.text: Wild animal tamed in London

definitions.meaning: Jack London's White Fang tells of such a creature gradually tamed

explanation.surface: A wild beast tamed in the English capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'London' is not the city but Jack London, whose White Fang is a part-dog wild animal domesticated.
explanation.definitionFit: The grey canine predator is a wild animal, and White Fang, tamed in Jack London's novel, is one.

clue.text: Powellian figure primed, perhaps, in cashmere

indicators.note: in means the shuffled letters go inside the word for the fabric

parts.note: cashmere is a fine wool

indicators.note: perhaps signals the word primed may be rearranged

explanation.surface: A character from Anthony Powell dressed, ready and prepared, in fine knitwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals the anagram and 'in' the container. Widmerpool is the pushy schemer of Anthony Powell's twelve-novel sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenneth Widmerpool is the ambitious figure running through Anthony Powell's A Dance to the Music of Time.

clue.text: Richard III as war hero, say

definitions.meaning: a nickname for the hunchbacked king
Guy, the hero of Evelyn Waugh's Second World War trilogy Sword of Honour

explanation.surface: Richard III imagined as a wartime hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard III was nicknamed for his supposed hunch, and Waugh's Guy of that surname is a soldier protagonist.

clue.text: Brussels schoolteacher confuses two rich Mrs.

indicators.note: confuses means the letters are jumbled into a different order

explanation.surface: A Belgian teacher muddles up two wealthy married women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confuses' rearranges TWORICHMRS. The teacher is the narrator of Charlotte Brontë's The Professor.
explanation.definitionFit: William Crimsworth teaches in Brussels in Charlotte Brontë's novel The Professor.

clue.text: Orate, and discover medical problem

indicators.note: problem suggests the word medical is in trouble, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Make a speech and find a health complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'medical problem' reads as an illness; 'problem' rearranges MEDICAL. 'and discover' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to speak in a grand, rhetorical way.

clue.text: Frame of Swinnerton's production

explanation.surface: A frame made by the novelist Swinnerton.
explanation.definitionFit: A hinged window sash is a frame, and Frank Swinnerton wrote a novel with that title.

clue.text: Qualification would suit Mountolive to "at"

indicators.note: the qualification would suit the character when a further letter is added, so his job title is shortened to give it

parts.note: Mountolive, in Durrell's Alexandria Quartet, is a British diplomat
the quoted at is read as 'a T': the answer ends in A and needs just a T added

explanation.surface: A certificate fit for the ambassador of Durrell's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Read '"at"' as 'a T': the qualification, which ends in A, gains a T to name Mountolive's profession, the ambassador in Lawrence Durrell's novel; 'to' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: A certificate awarded for completing a course is an academic qualification.

clue.text: Flatter Civil War digger?

definitions.meaning: one that flattens or makes things even
a member of a radical English Civil War faction, close kin to the Diggers

explanation.surface: Asking whether a seventeenth-century digger was more level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flatter' looks like a verb meaning praise or an adjective, but is one who flattens. The Levellers and Diggers were radical groups of the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who makes things even is one, and the Civil War radicals took that same name.

clue.text: Sitting at the College of Arms

definitions.text: Sitting at the College of Arms

parts.words: Sitting at the College of Arms
parts.note: the heralds' word for a beast seated upright on a coat of arms

explanation.surface: Someone taking a seat at the heraldic authority's office.
explanation.walkthrough: The College of Arms is the English body regulating heraldry, so this is the heraldic term for sitting.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry a beast shown seated on its haunches is described with this Norman-French term.

clue.text: They featured in Adcock's Idylls

parts.note: A. St John Adcock's stories were titled East End Idylls, about poor London residents

explanation.surface: A remark about the characters in some idyllic poems.
explanation.walkthrough: Adcock's book of London sketches is East End Idylls, so its people come from that district of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Residents of London's East End are the subjects of Adcock's East End Idylls.

clue.text: Edit Ovid? There's nothing in it

indicators.note: edit means the poet's name is reworked, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Revising a Roman poet's work turns out to be pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edit' rearranges OVID.
explanation.definitionFit: An empty space or vacuum is one that holds nothing at all.

clue.text: Bury in the works of eighteenth-century historian

parts.note: taken as written
David Hume wrote a History of England in the eighteenth century

explanation.surface: Immerse yourself in a Scottish historian's books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the works of' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter a body is to place it in the ground.

clue.text: Agnes, who went far with Forster

definitions.text: Agnes, who went far with Forster

parts.words: Agnes, who went far with Forster
parts.note: Agnes appears in Forster's The Longest Journey, so 'went far' hints at the title

explanation.surface: A woman travelling a long way with the novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went far' points to Forster's novel The Longest Journey, in which Agnes marries the hero Rickie.
explanation.definitionFit: Agnes, the hero's wife in Forster's The Longest Journey, has this surname.

clue.text: Forerunner of CIA reaches a high point in Greece

parts.note: the OSS, Office of Strategic Services, was the wartime precursor of the CIA

explanation.surface: An American spy agency's predecessor reaches a summit in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reaches' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: The mountain in Thessaly, piled on Pelion by the giants, is a Greek peak.

clue.text: Meditative emperor

parts.note: the Roman emperor who wrote the Stoic Meditations

explanation.surface: A thoughtful ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: Marcus Aurelius wrote the Meditations, so 'Meditative' points to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor, wrote the Stoic Meditations.

clue.text: His kingdom ravaged by threat attributable to swine

definitions.text: His kingdom ravaged by threat attributable to swine

parts.words: His kingdom ravaged by threat attributable to swine
parts.note: the Calydonian boar was sent by Artemis to lay waste the realm of the king who forgot her sacrifice

explanation.surface: A king whose realm is laid waste by a pig.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Artemis sent a giant boar against Calydon because its king neglected her offering.
explanation.definitionFit: The king of Calydon neglected Artemis, who loosed the Calydonian boar on his land.

clue.text: Weak leading men opposed to Carlyle's theme?

parts.note: anti means against
Carlyle lectured On Heroes, Hero-Worship and the Heroic in History

explanation.surface: Feeble principal actors set against Carlyle's subject.
explanation.walkthrough: Carlyle's On Heroes celebrates great men, so his theme is the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Protagonists lacking conventional heroic virtues are flawed central characters.
